clue.text: The fellow savaged article advocating opposing point of view

parts.note: a fellow is a man, and the pronoun for him is he

indicators.note: to savage something is to tear it to pieces, so the letters of the word that follows are pulled apart and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written: these seven letters are the ones rearranged

explanation.surface: A man tears into a piece of journalism that argued for the other side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'savaged' tears the letters of 'article' apart and reassembles them as RETICAL. That word usually signals A, AN or THE, but here it is the raw material itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive phrase for the adjective: heretical writing argues against orthodox or established doctrine, promoting the contrary belief.

clue.text: Finally had a tea where the samovar is?

indicators.note: finally points to the end of the word that follows, so only its closing letter is kept

parts.note: cha is an informal British word for tea, also spelt char

explanation.surface: Someone at last gets a cup of tea in the room where the Russian urn stands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' takes the last letter of 'had', D. The question mark admits the definition is only a likely setting: a samovar is a Russian tea urn, at home in a Russian country cottage.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a samovar is a Russian tea urn, and a dacha is a Russian country cottage where one would be kept.

clue.text: Second course: arrangement of pancakes?

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for second, the unit of time
a tack is the course a sailing boat steers relative to the wind, and so any line of action

explanation.surface: The next dish on the menu: pancakes, nicely laid out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second course' reads as one menu phrase but splits into two separate pieces. The question mark shows pancakes are only one example of things piled up.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: pancakes are traditionally served piled one on top of another, and such a pile is a stack.

clue.text: Unhappy Moroccans ignoring new opening for Morocco in wider world picture

indicators.note: unhappy suggests something upset or out of sorts, so the letters that follow are disturbed into a different order
ignoring means leaving something out, so one letter is dropped from the word before it

parts.note: taken as written, before one letter is dropped
N is the standard abbreviation for new, as in NT for New Testament

indicators.note: the opening for a word is the letter it starts with, the only one taken

explanation.surface: Discontented Moroccans overlook a fresh chance for their country on the global stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignoring' drops N from MOROCCANS, 'Unhappy' rearranges the remaining MOROCCAS into MACROCOS, and 'opening for' adds the M of 'Morocco'. 'in' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: the macrocosm is the universe, or any great whole, seen as the large-scale counterpart of a smaller system within it.

clue.text: Bouquet, expressing love: stylish and having remarkable power

indicators.note: to express is also to squeeze or press out, as juice is expressed from fruit, so one letter is pushed out of the word before it

parts.note: a posy is a small bunch of flowers, a bouquet
love is a score of zero in tennis, and zero looks like the letter O
chic means elegantly fashionable, stylish

explanation.surface: A bunch of flowers that declares affection, looks elegant and makes a striking impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'expressing' means squeezing out, not declaring: POSY loses its O (love, the tennis score of zero) to leave PSY. 'and' joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Description of the adjective: a psychic person is credited with paranormal abilities such as telepathy or clairvoyance, powers beyond the ordinary.

clue.text: American writer, having put out book, remains active

indicators.note: to put something out is to eject it, so the word that comes next has one letter removed

parts.note: embers are the glowing remains of a fire
an appliance that is on is switched on and working, so on can mean active

explanation.surface: A US author who has published a new title is still busy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having put out' removes B from EMBERS, leaving EMERS. 'remains' is a noun here, what a fire leaves, not the verb of the surface; Ralph Waldo Emerson was a 19th-century American essayist and poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Example by name: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803-82) was a US essayist, poet and leading Transcendentalist thinker.

clue.text: Expected blow? Pressure gets Minister, feeling bad, to deviate

parts.note: P is the symbol for pressure in physics
Rev is short for Reverend, the title of a minister of the church
someone ailing is unwell, feeling bad
a road that winds twists and turns away from a straight line, so to wind, with a long i, is to deviate

explanation.surface: A setback was foreseen: lobbying makes a guilty government minister change course.
explanation.walkthrough: Four pieces follow one another, with 'gets' as a link. The last is the verb with a long 'i' (a path winds), though the answer uses the noun; the question mark flags 'blow' as a playful word for moving air.
explanation.definitionFit: Playful description: the wind that most usually blows over a region is the one you would anticipate, and a wind is literally a blow of air.

clue.text: Contemporary location attracting crowd to a hanging?

definitions.text: Contemporary location attracting crowd to a hanging?

parts.words: Contemporary location attracting crowd to a hanging?
parts.note: crowds once gathered to watch public executions; the hangings that draw the public today are paintings put up on walls for display

explanation.surface: A present-day venue where people flock to watch an execution.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay, only a playful description. 'Hanging' suggests an execution, which once drew crowds; 'Contemporary' points instead to today's hangings, paintings displayed on walls.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic description: a hanging is also an exhibition of paintings on walls, and the building the public visits to view them is this.

clue.text: Encouraging reduction in staff and employment

indicators.note: a reduction in a word makes it shorter, so the word that follows loses its last letter

parts.note: a staff is a long stick or rod
the employment of a tool is the using of it

explanation.surface: Someone is in favour of cutting both the workforce and the number of jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduction in' shortens ROD to RO by dropping its last letter. The surface's staff are employees, but the wordplay wants a stick; 'and' simply joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a participle: rousing people is stirring them to action or raising their spirits, as a stirring speech does.

clue.text: Men and graduate admitted by academic, one controlling entrance

indicators.note: whatever is admitted by something is let inside it, so the first two pieces go within the third

parts.note: a don is a university teacher, especially at Oxford or Cambridge
OR stands for other ranks, the British Army's term for its soldiers (men) who are not officers
MA is Master of Arts, a degree held by a graduate

explanation.surface: An admissions tutor lets some chaps and a degree-holder into the college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admitted by' lets the first two pieces inside the academic, just ahead of its last letter. The surface is about university admissions, but 'Men' are soldiers: OR is 'other ranks', British troops who are not officers.
explanation.definitionFit: Job description: a doorman stands at the entry to a hotel, club or block of flats and decides who may come in.

clue.text: Worry about staff attached to the French port

indicators.note: attached to means fastened on, so what has been built so far is joined directly to the piece that follows
about means around, so the first piece is wrapped round the second

parts.note: to fret is to worry
to staff a post is to man it, to supply the people who work there
le is the French word for the, in its masculine form

explanation.surface: There is concern over the employees posted to the harbour in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the worry round the staff, and 'attached to' fastens the French article on the end. 'French' belongs to the wordplay, so the port need not be in France: Fremantle is the harbour of Perth, Western Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Example of the category: Fremantle is the main harbour city of Western Australia, at the mouth of the Swan River near Perth.

clue.text: Areas of ground in which University's planted flower

indicators.note: in which points back to the first piece as the place where the next one goes
something planted is set into the ground, so the single letter is set inside the first piece

parts.note: lots are plots of land, as in building lots
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Plots of land where a university has bedded out a bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in which' and 'planted' together put U inside LOTS. The apostrophe-s means 'has' in the surface but 'is' in the wordplay: U is planted.
explanation.definitionFit: Member of the category: the lotus is a water lily with large showy blooms, sacred in Buddhism and Hinduism.

clue.text: Prickly sensation hasn't left touch

indicators.note: hasn't says the word before it lacks what is named next, so one letter is taken out

parts.note: a tingle is a slight prickling or stinging feeling

explanation.surface: Pins and needles linger in someone's sense of touch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hasn't' takes L (left) out of TINGLE. In the surface 'left' means departed and 'touch' is the sense of feeling; the definition wants touch as a slight trace, as in a touch of colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a noun: a tinge is a slight trace or hint of something, especially of colour, just as a touch of red is.

clue.text: Hard-working donkey is carrying two with minimum of unease

parts.note: an ass is a donkey

indicators.note: to carry is to hold a load, so the word before it has the next two pieces placed inside it

parts.note: a duo is a pair, two people performing together

indicators.note: a loose signal: the minimum of a word is its smallest possible part, a single letter, and by convention that is the first

explanation.surface: A diligent beast of burden bears a pair of riders without the slightest fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying' puts DUO and U inside IS, after ASS. 'minimum of' is a loose signal: the least bit of 'unease' is a single letter, by convention its first; 'with' just joins the inner pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an assiduous worker is diligent and persevering, showing constant careful effort.

clue.text: Sulk during house visit — something in the garden?

indicators.note: during means in the course of, so the sulk goes inside the phrase that follows it, landing within the second of its two words

parts.note: to see someone is to visit them, as in going to see a friend
the pip is dated British slang for a fit of bad temper or low spirits, as in it gives me the pip

explanation.surface: Someone mopes all through a call at a friend's home; there is something out in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' drops the sulk into 'house visit' read as one run of letters, where it lands in the second word. That sulk is PIP: 'the pip' is dated British slang for a fit of ill humour, which the setter stretches to cover sulking.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a hosepipe is the flexible tube used for watering lawns and flower beds.

clue.text: Some bread? Yes

indicators.note: some means a part of, so the answer is a run of letters lying inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Offered a slice or two from the loaf, someone accepts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' marks a run of letters spanning 'bread' and 'Yes'. The whole clue also defines the answer: bread is slang for money, and 'the ready' (or 'readies') is British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang synonym read from the whole clue: bread is money, and ready, as in 'the ready' or readies, is British slang for cash in hand.

clue.text: Become bold: how to kill vampire with decapitation?

indicators.note: decapitation is beheading, so the phrase before it loses its first letter

parts.note: in vampire lore the way to destroy one is to drive a wooden stake through its heart; this is the first word of that terse two-word instruction, the weapon
the second word of the same terse instruction: the organ that the wooden point has to pierce

explanation.surface: Find your courage: here is the way to finish off a vampire by cutting off its head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with decapitation' beheads the instruction STAKE HEART, removing its S. The surface suggests cutting off the vampire's head, but it is the phrase that loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to take heart is to gain courage or confidence, to feel emboldened by something.

clue.text: Mineral in soft drink mostly? That's absurd

indicators.note: in says the first piece sits inside the shortened second one
mostly means most of the word is used, so it loses its last letter

parts.note: cola is a sweet fizzy soft drink
mica is a shiny silicate mineral that splits into thin sheets

explanation.surface: The idea that a fizzy pop is largely made of rock is dismissed as ridiculous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims the soft drink to COL, and 'in' puts the mineral within it. In Britain 'minerals' can also mean fizzy soft drinks, so the surface reads naturally; 'That's' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Near-synonym: something comical is laughable or ludicrous, which is one sense of absurd.

clue.text: Energy conserver initially replacing article in lamp stand

indicators.note: replacing means taking the place of, so the two letters built first are swapped in for the article
in says the article to be swapped out is found inside the word for lamp

parts.note: a lantern is a lamp with a protective case
an is the indefinite article used before a vowel
E is the symbol for energy in physics

indicators.note: initially points to the initial, the first letter, of the word before it

explanation.surface: A power-saving device is fitted at first in place of an item in a standard lamp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes C from 'conserver'; 'replacing' and 'in' put E and C where the article sits in the lamp. 'Lamp stand' wants to be the definition; only 'stand' is.
explanation.definitionFit: Example of the category: a lectern is a tall sloping-topped desk that holds a book or notes for a reader or speaker.

clue.text: First medic's buzzer?

parts.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor, a medic
the first in a numbered series is number one, and a title is written before the number, as on a nameplate

explanation.surface: The pager belonging to the earliest doctor on the scene.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'First medic' as a title, Dr One, title before number, which is why the pieces swap order. The question mark excuses the whimsy: a male bee is something that buzzes.
explanation.definitionFit: Whimsical description: a drone is a male honeybee, an insect that buzzes; the word also means a low humming noise.

clue.text: Colonies abroad importing new enamelware

indicators.note: to import is to bring in, so the rearranged letters take one more letter inside them
abroad can mean widely scattered or astray, so the letters of the word before it are scattered into a different order

parts.note: taken as written: these eight letters are rearranged
N is the standard abbreviation for new, as in NT for New Testament

explanation.surface: Overseas territories are buying in a fresh consignment of enamelled goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' rearranges COLONIES into CLOISONE and 'importing' takes N (new) inside. Cloisonné, French for 'partitioned', is enamel work whose colours are kept apart by thin metal strips.
explanation.definitionFit: Type of the thing: cloisonné is decorative work in which coloured enamels fill cells divided by fine wire on a metal base.

clue.text: Fish topped with last of roasted nut

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its top, so in this down entry the word before it loses its first letter

parts.note: a salmon is a large fish prized for its pink flesh

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, the only one taken

explanation.surface: A fish dish garnished with the final roasted nut left in the bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topped' removes the S of SALMON, leaving ALMON, and 'last of' takes the D of 'roasted'. In the surface 'topped with' means garnished; in a down entry topping is losing the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Member of the category: the almond is the edible oval kernel of a tree related to the peach, sold and eaten as a nut.

clue.text: Decorated urn — a piece appealing to the connoisseur?

indicators.note: to decorate is to dress something up and change how it looks, so the letters that follow are given a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An ornamented vase: just the item a discerning collector would love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decorated' rearranges URN, A and PIECE; the dash is only punctuation. An epicure is a connoisseur of food and drink, and the question mark allows the stretch to anything refined.
explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive phrase: an epicure is a person of refined taste, especially in food and wine, so epicurean things suit such a discerning palate.

clue.text: Source of water I directed after nothing's drunk

indicators.note: after sends the two pieces named before it, the pronoun and the verb, behind the piece named next

parts.note: a well is a shaft sunk into the ground to reach water
nothing is zero, which looks like the letter O
led means guided or directed, as a conductor led the orchestra

explanation.surface: With not a drop yet drunk, I pointed the way to a spring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' reorders the middle of the answer: what 'I directed' gives comes behind what 'nothing' gives. In the surface 'drunk' is a verb form (nothing has been drunk); the definition is the adjective meaning intoxicated.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang synonym: well-oiled is an informal British way of saying someone is intoxicated, tipsy with alcohol.

clue.text: Fellow's holding on with spy, struggling, going under

indicators.note: to hold is to contain, so the first piece keeps the rearranged letters inside it

parts.note: what is the fellow's belongs to him: it is his

indicators.note: struggling suggests thrashing about, so the letters of the two words before it are thrown into a different order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man clings on beside a secret agent, fighting to stay afloat as he sinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'struggling' rearranges 'on' and 'spy' into YPNOS, and 'holding' puts that within the fellow's word; 'with' only joins the two. 'Going under' suggests drowning, but it is what a hypnotist's subject does.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose noun phrase: a subject entering a trance is said to go under, so the process of being put into that sleep-like state fits.

clue.text: River, say, and a series of races — a _______

definitions.text: River, say, and a series of races — a _______

parts.note: R is the standard map abbreviation for river
eg, short for the Latin exempli gratia, means for example, or say
the TT, or Tourist Trophy, is a series of motorcycle races held each year on the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank question about a waterway and a programme of races.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is wordplay and definition at once: the blank stands for the answer, a programme of boat races, often on a river. TT is the Tourist Trophy, motorcycle races held yearly on the Isle of Man.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes it: a regatta is a sporting event made up of several boat or yacht contests, typically on a river or lake.

clue.text: Follow up news department's outing King and attractive woman

indicators.note: in a down entry up means reading from the bottom towards the top, so the word before it is written backwards

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely

indicators.note: outing is read as putting out, so one letter is ejected from the word before it

parts.note: the news desk is the department of a newspaper or broadcaster that handles news, and the possessive makes it desk's
K is the abbreviation for king in chess and cards

explanation.surface: Chase up the newsroom's story exposing the private lives of a monarch and a beautiful lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns DOG into GOD in this down entry, and 'outing' removes K (King) from DESKS to leave DESS. 'and' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative synonym: a woman adored for her beauty is called a goddess, as in a screen goddess.

clue.text: One researching, perhaps form of magnetism for gain

parts.note: a prof, short for professor, is a senior academic who may well carry out research; perhaps admits that not every researcher is one
it is old slang for sex appeal, magnetism of a personal sort, as in the It girl

explanation.surface: A scientist looks into a type of magnetic effect in the hope of making money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' is old slang for sex appeal, magnetism of a personal sort, as in the 'It girl'. 'perhaps' admits a professor is only one example of a researcher; 'for' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as noun or verb: a profit is money made or an advantage won, and to profit is to benefit.

clue.text: I'm to carry on erasing first picture

parts.note: taken as written, without its apostrophe

indicators.note: erasing first means rubbing out the first letter of the word just given

parts.note: to wage is to carry on or conduct, as in waging war or a campaign

explanation.surface: I intend to keep going, rubbing out my earliest drawing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'erasing first' removes the W of WAGE (to carry on, as in wage war), leaving AGE. The surface makes 'first picture' one phrase, but 'first' belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an image is a likeness or visual representation, such as a photograph or drawing.

clue.text: Way of working, penning extravagant epigram

indicators.note: to pen is to shut in, as sheep are penned, so the first piece encloses the second

parts.note: MO is short for modus operandi, Latin for a way of working
OTT is short for over the top, an informal British phrase meaning excessive or extravagant

explanation.surface: A writer's method: composing a lavishly worded witty saying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penning' looks like writing but means enclosing, as sheep are penned: MO goes round OTT. OTT is the informal British abbreviation of 'over the top', meaning excessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Near-synonym: a motto is a short pithy saying expressing a guiding principle, much as an epigram is a brief pointed remark.
